guide_description: Three days along the Amalfi Coast covering its three distinct characters: the medieval maritime republic at the center, the vertical fishing-village glamour of the western coast, and the aristocratic hilltop gardens above the sea. Each cluster is geographically self-contained and connected by ferry or coastal road.

days.cluster_tagline: A medieval maritime republic packed into a single ravine - cathedral, cloister, and a secret neighboring village
days.neighborhood_description: Amalfi was one of the four great maritime republics of medieval Italy, trading with Constantinople and North Africa long before Venice rose to prominence. Today the town is compressed into the mouth of the Valle dei Mulini, with its Arab-Norman cathedral dominating the main piazza. Atrani, a five-minute walk east around the headland, is a genuine working village that most day-trippers entirely miss.

morning.notes: Arrive before 9:30am when the ferry day-trippers from Positano and Salerno flood the piazza. The 62-step staircase facade is Norman-Arab-Byzantine in style - a hybrid that reflects Amalfi's trading networks across the medieval Mediterranean. The entry ticket includes the Chiostro del Paradiso, a 13th-century cloister with interlaced Arab arches, and the crypt of Saint Andrew. The bronze doors were cast in Constantinople around 1066.

afternoon.notes: Amalfi produced some of the earliest European paper in the 13th century and this working mill in the Valle dei Mulini still demonstrates the process using the original water-hammer system. The walk up the valley from Piazza Duomo takes about ten minutes through a narrow gorge that is genuinely cool on a hot day - useful in July and August. The museum is small but the demonstration is specific and not available anywhere else on the coast.

evening.activity_title: Atrani village and Piazza Umberto I
evening.notes: Atrani is Italy's smallest municipality by area and it shows - the entire village wraps around one tiny piazza that sits a meter above the beach. Walk from Amalfi via the coastal path rather than the road: exit east along the waterfront promenade, pass under the arch cut into the cliff, and you arrive from the sea side. Eat here rather than in Amalfi - the restaurants on and around Piazza Umberto I are less than half the price for the same fish.

if_time_permits.activity_title: Church of Santa Maria Assunta - Atrani
if_time_permits.notes: The church at the top of Atrani's staircase holds the original bronze doors from Constantinople, cast in 1086 - predating Amalfi Cathedral's doors by a generation. Almost no one climbs up to see them, which makes it the quietest significant medieval object on the coast.

The waterfront square named for Flavio Gioia, the Amalfitan credited with introducing the magnetic compass to Europe. The claim is disputed by historians, but the arsenal vaults along the western edge are real - the 12th-century maritime warehouses where Amalfi's war galleys were built and stored, now converted to an exhibition space.

days.cluster_tagline: Vertiginous fishing villages stacked on cliffs - pastel houses, church domes, and the coast's best swimming coves
days.neighborhood_description: Positano is the most photographed village on the coast, its pastel houses cascading down a near-vertical cliff to a black-sand beach. The crowds are real but manageable before 11am and after 5pm. Praiano, three kilometers east along the Nastro Azzurro, is smaller, quieter, and sits higher on the cliff with a different angle on the sea - the place Positano visitors drive past without stopping.

morning.activity_title: Positano - Chiesa di Santa Maria Assunta
morning.notes: The majolica-tiled dome visible in every photograph of Positano is this church, sitting just above the beach. Inside is a 13th-century Byzantine icon of the Black Madonna, the object around which the entire village's founding legend turns. Go early - the church is small and the interior is dark and cool. The walk down from the main road to the church through the village staircase alleys is the best introduction to Positano's spatial logic.

afternoon.activity_title: Spiaggia Grande and the Positano cliffside
afternoon.notes: The beach itself is crowded and the sun beds expensive - the free section is at the far eastern end near the ferry dock. The more rewarding afternoon activity is climbing back up through the village via Via dei Mulini and Via Cristoforo Colombo rather than the main Via Pasitea. These narrower staircases pass through working residential layers of Positano that the boutique strip never shows.

evening.activity_title: Praiano and Marina di Praia cove
evening.notes: Praiano sits at a higher elevation than Positano and faces slightly more southwest, which makes the sunset view across to Capri cleaner and less obstructed. Marina di Praia is a tiny cove 150 steps below the main road - take the staircase signed from the SS163 and you reach a narrow beach enclosed by two cliff faces with a couple of restaurants where the tables are practically in the water. The last ferry back to Amalfi or Positano runs around 6pm in shoulder season; check times before you commit to staying for dinner.

if_time_permits.activity_title: Path of the Gods - western trailhead at Nocelle
if_time_permits.notes: The Sentiero degli Dei runs along the cliff above Positano from Bomerano to Nocelle - the full trail is a 7.8km one-way hike. If you only have an hour, take the local bus from Positano center to Nocelle and walk the first kilometer east along the ridge. The views down onto Positano and the Faraglioni sea stacks are the best available on the coast without a boat.

walk_from_main_route.from: Positano - Chiesa di Santa Maria Assunta

days.cluster_tagline: An aristocratic hilltop town 350 meters above the sea - two villa gardens and the quietest views on the coast
days.neighborhood_description: Ravello sits on a ridge above the Valle del Dragone, accessible by a winding road from Atrani or by bus from Amalfi. The town was a Norman feudal capital and later a refuge for Wagner, DH Lawrence, and Gore Vidal. Its two great villas - Rufolo and Cimbrone - have gardens that project over the cliff edge with unobstructed views across the Tyrrhenian sea. The town itself is small enough to cover entirely on foot.

morning.notes: Built in the 13th century by a Ravello merchant family wealthy enough to bankroll three popes, the villa was ruined and overgrown by the 19th century when Scottish botanist Francis Neville Reid restored it. Wagner visited in 1880 and declared the Moorish courtyard was the garden of Klingsor from Parsifal - the festival held here every summer is named for that visit. Go early before the tour buses arrive at 10am; the tower is the best single viewpoint and gets crowded fast.

afternoon.notes: Founded in 1086 and rebuilt several times since - the facade is a 1930s reconstruction, but the interior holds two 12th-century marble ambos that are among the finest examples of Romanesque decorative carving in southern Italy. The ambo on the right, commissioned by Nicola Rufolo in 1272, features mosaic-inlaid columns supported by six lions and a carved relief of Jonah and the whale that reads almost as proto-Gothic sculpture.

evening.notes: The Belvedere dell'Infinito at the garden's southern tip is a terrace lined with 18th-century marble busts sitting on the cliff edge at 350 meters, with an unobstructed drop to the sea and a view stretching from Capo Palinuro to Capri. Gore Vidal described it as the most beautiful view in the world. Arrive at least 90 minutes before sunset to walk the full garden first - the English landscape layout includes a Temple of Bacchus, a rose garden, and a crypt - then position yourself on the terrace for the light change. The path from Ravello Piazza to the villa entrance is entirely on foot, past private villas and no road traffic.

if_time_permits.notes: A concrete concert hall designed by Oscar Niemeyer and completed in 2010, cantilevered over the cliff edge at the north end of Ravello's piazza. Controversial when built for disrupting the medieval townscape, it has since become an architectural landmark in its own right. The exterior terrace is freely accessible and gives a different angle - looking north toward Maiori - from anything the historic center offers.

if_time_permits.activity_title: Scala village and Santa Caterina church
if_time_permits.notes: Scala is Ravello's older neighbor on the opposite side of the Valle del Dragone - it was the bishop's seat before Ravello and is almost entirely unvisited. A 25-minute walk west from Ravello along the ridge path passes through terraced lemon groves and arrives at a village where the 12th-century cathedral facade is still in its original form. The path itself is the draw: it runs along the ridge between 400 and 450 meters with both the Tyrrhenian coast and the mountains behind visible simultaneously.
